title: Expert consensus on core terminology in the field of forest and nature therapy.
summary:
Nature-based interventions—especially structured forest stays—have received growing scientific attention internationally over the past two decades. Studies, primarily from Japan and South Korea, point to physiological effects, including reductions in cortisol levels, blood pressure, and heart rate, as well as increased activity of natural killer cells (Li 2010; Park et al. 2010). Psychological effects such as stress reduction, improved mood, and increased attention span have also been documented (Ideno et al. 2017; Siah et al. 2023). The WHO has explicitly recognized nature-based interventions as a relevant tool for health promotion and prevention in its Global Action Plans (WHO 2021; WHO 2022). Nevertheless, the field of research is methodologically heterogeneous: different types of interventions, dosages, settings, and study populations make it difficult to compare study results and limit the possibilities for evidence synthesis.
Despite growing empirical evidence, there is still no internationally agreed, standardized terminology for the field of forest and nature therapy. Terms such as forest therapy, shinrin-yoku, forest bathing, forest medicine, nature-based therapy, and forest bathing are used in the literature sometimes synonymously, sometimes with diverging meanings (Park et al. 2010; Li 2010; Ideno et al. 2017; Siah et al. 2023). A systematic analysis of existing definitions shows that neither the criteria for distinguishing between the different forms of intervention nor hierarchical classifications of terms have been consistently established in the literature. This terminological ambiguity has direct consequences: it complicates the operationalization of interventions in clinical studies, limits the reproducibility of findings, prevents valid meta-analyses, and hinders the development of guidelines and the integration of nature-based offerings into the health system. A similar situation existed in the field of fasting research before Breinlinger et al. (2023) developed an internationally agreed fasting terminology using a modified Delphi method. No such consensus project has yet been undertaken for the field of forest and nature therapy.
This raises the following question: Which core concepts and definitions in the field of nature and forest therapy can be agreed upon through a structured international consensus of experts using a modified Delphi method, and how can these be transferred into a hierarchical taxonomic structure? As a secondary question, we will examine which of these internationally agreed terms and definitions can be adapted linguistically and culturally for the DACH region through a subsequent German-language Delphi process.
A uniform, internationally recognized core terminology forms the necessary basis for methodologically precise clinical studies, for the comparability of intervention types, and for the development of evidence-based guidelines in the field of nature-based health interventions. In addition, agreed terminology supports interdisciplinary communication between medicine, psychology, forestry science, and public health, as well as the integration of these interventions into health policy and healthcare provision. Last but not least, the project represents a structural prerequisite for the research field's compatibility with international standardization processes, such as those of the WHO or ISO (WHO 2021; WHO 2022).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•	At least five peer-reviewed scientific publications in the field of forest and nature therapy, forest medicine, or related nature-based interventions in English (first or last author)
or
•	At least one relevant publication (e.g., peer-reviewed article, gray literature, co- or first authorship, book contribution, reference book, or training manual) and at least five years of clinical therapeutic experience in the relevant field.
Exclusion criteria:
•	Lack of thematic expertise in the field of nature-based or forest-based interventions,
•	Exclusively administrative work without technical involvement
•	Relevant conflicts of interest that could compromise independent assessment
•	unwillingness to participate.
